analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by members of Congress and top officials, restricts family lobbying and corporate board seats, and bars foreign lobbying after office.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 5 cosponsors, the bill was referred to four committees and has received no vote or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children from trading individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets, unless the investments sit in a qualified blind trust; diversified index funds and Treasury bonds would still be allowed. Violators would give up any profits and face penalties of up to three times the value of the trade, published publicly. It would also ban former members and Senate-confirmed officials from ever lobbying for China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or other designated countries; require spouses of senior officials to register and file quarterly reports if they do paid advocacy work; bar members and their spouses from serving on for-profit corporate boards; and extend congressional gift rules to spouses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a government whose elected officials cannot personally profit from individual stock, commodity, crypto, or futures trades while writing laws, and can see violations published online. It also limits the revolving door for lobbying on behalf of rival foreign powers and closes the loophole that lets officeholders' spouses do paid influence work without registering as lobbyists.

how_it_helps.text: Bans the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, candidates, and their spouses and dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets, unless held in a qualified blind trust; diversified index funds and Treasuries are still allowed.

Attaches penalties to violations — surrender of profits plus up to triple the value of the trade — and requires ethics offices to publish each violation and penalty online, with officials barred from paying fines out of office accounts or campaign donations.
Imposes a lifetime ban on former Members and Senate-confirmed officials lobbying or advising for China, North Korea, Russia, Iran, or any country the Secretary of State designates a concern.

Requires spouses of Members and Senate-confirmed officials to register and file quarterly reports on paid advocacy work that leans on their access, with civil fines up to $200,000 and criminal penalties for knowing violations.

Bars Members and their spouses from serving on for-profit corporate boards, with disclosure requirements for pre-existing board seats, and extends House and Senate gift rules to cover Members' spouses.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, their spouses and children (who lose the ability to trade individual securities and sit on corporate boards and must disclose advocacy work), plus lobbying firms and former officials who monetize foreign-government access, and brokerages that profit from congressional trading.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The stock-trading ban forces Members to move investments into blind trusts or diversified funds, giving up control over their own finances — a real burden the bill imposes on officeholders and their families.

The lifetime foreign-lobbying ban reaches candidate spouses and dependent children and bars conduct after office for life, raising fair-notice and enforceability questions courts or future Congresses could contest.

The spouse registration and quarterly-disclosure regime imposes new reporting obligations on private citizens who did not choose to run for office, which critics argue intrudes on family members' own careers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would close well-documented gaps — members trading individual stocks, spouses lobbying without registering, former officials representing hostile foreign governments — at a real but manageable cost to officials' and their families' financial freedom. The trading ban's carve-outs (diversified index funds, Treasuries) give officials ample ways to save, and public objections are mostly about the loss of investment flexibility and Second Amendment-adjacent concerns, not about ordinary people being harmed. On balance the public benefit of removing financial conflicts from lawmaking outweighs the cost to officials' personal finances.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four committees, none of which ever acted on it, so it died without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Haley Stevens introduced the No Getting Rich in Congress Act on March 5, 2026.
The bill was referred the same day to four committees: House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Rules.
No committee has reported the bill, and no floor vote has occurred; the only actions on record are introduction and referral.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families keep the ability to trade individual stocks and serve on corporate boards while in office, and former officials remain free to lobby for designated foreign governments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and their families

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support is on record.

industries.industry: Foreign lobbying and government-relations firms working for China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea
industries.note: The bill makes it a crime for former Members and confirmed officials to represent designated foreign countries of concern, cutting off a lucrative post-office career path.

industries.industry: Spouses of officeholders who sell advocacy access
industries.note: Spousal lobbying currently falls outside the Lobbying Disclosure Act; the bill requires registration, quarterly disclosure, and penalties, closing a channel through which access to power has been monetized.

Members' individual-stock trading, which generates fees and is a marketing point for some firms, would be restricted to blind trusts and diversified funds; broad index-fund investing remains unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with four committees and no Republican cosponsors; similar congressional stock-trading bans have repeatedly stalled in past Congresses. Without bipartisan sponsorship or a committee schedule, it is very unlikely to receive a vote this Congress.
